web_evidence.title: Interview with Mary Stewart
web_evidence.note: In a University of Rochester-hosted author interview, Stewart says she returned to first-person narrative and retained it until the Mordred novel The Wicked Day; she also explicitly identifies Merlin as the narrator recalling his youth in The Crystal Cave.

web_evidence.title: Im-mortality: The Literary Death and Rebirth of King Arthur and His Kingdom
web_evidence.note: This Ca' Foscari University master's thesis identifies Stewart's chosen voice as a first-person narrator and analyzes Merlin's retrospective narration, quoting the novel's first-person opening.

web_evidence.title: The Crystal Cave by Mary Stewart — MonkeyNotes
web_evidence.note: The study guide explicitly states that the entire point of view is first person and that Merlin is the narrator.

web_evidence.title: The Crystal Cave by Mary Stewart
web_evidence.note: Distributed text snippets show first-person openings for the prologue and Books I–III, Merlin's commentary on the chronicles at the opening of Book IV, and first-person narration in the ending.

web_evidence.title: Mary Stewart Writing Styles in The Crystal Cave
web_evidence.note: This guide describes both first- and third-person passages, citing Book IV, Chapter 1; however, it also says Merlin himself tells the third-person account of Ambrosius's exploits, indicating embedded historical storytelling rather than a separate controlling narrator.

person_note: Merlin is the controlling retrospective narrator and a participant in the story. Multiple event quotes independently expose his I/my voice, especially the explicit old-man frame in q01742; dialogue and gnomic quotations were excluded, while the two isolated third-person scene fragments remain unmarked. The author interview, academic thesis, and whole-book study guide corroborate first-person narration. BookRags uses 'third person' for historical passages about events Merlin did not witness, chiefly Book IV, Chapter 1, but explicitly attributes that storytelling to Merlin; the named-book openings likewise preserve his retrospective framing. Those passages are therefore embedded historical recounting by the same participating narrator, not an autonomous third-person base section. The only minor uncertainty is the extent of those historical stretches, with no credible evidence of a separate controlling narrator.
